newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr recoups losses, reinforces range.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr recoups losses, reinforces range.

text.p: The Australian dollar bounced back Monday as early U.S. and Japan sales were soaked up by Asian and exporter bids catching bears in a nasty short squeeze. In a blow by blow replay of every session last week the currency first tested support as concerns over its shrinking yield advantage soured sentiment. But true to form, demand was healthy around US$0.7730 and it was soon relaxing at US$0.7765.

There was also talk of a respected Swiss name on either side of the action, lending credence to rumours of a large strangle option which have been bedevelling the market for more than a week and adding to the general range-bound mentality.

By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was reclining at US$0.7770/75 after dipping as deep as US$0.7734 this morning. It was also up on the US$0.7756/61 level held late Thursday before the local market shut for the ANZAC Day holiday.
But neither did the currency seriously trouble US$0.7795 resistance, a barrier which capped it for all of last week, and dealers were resigned to a few more days of sideways drift.

The pattern was similar on the crosses where it initially ran into sizeable selling, but as the day wore on good buying emerged from Tokyo and ushered it up to 98.50/60 yen from an early 98.10/20 and 98.00/10 late here Thursday.
The dollar bloc also benefited from a rather tamely-worded communique from the G7 heads, who were gathered in Washington for yet another summit.

Various officials said the U.S. had agreed with Japan that a further rise in the dollar was not appropriate and currencies should trade in line with fundamentals. They did not, however, discuss any concrete plan for restraining the U.S. dollar and dealers felt fundamentals fully supported a firmer currency.
In particular, above trend growth in the U.S. meant the Federal Reserve was likely to tighten policy again next month, making the dollar a more attractive investment.
The dollar was up at 1.7323/28 marks and 126.75/85 yen from 1.7270/80 and 126.20/30 late in New York Friday.
The local currency followed against the mark to reach 1.3458/70 from 1.3323/37 late here Thursday, and to 60.4 on its trade weighted index from 60.1.
In contrast to the U.S. the risk in Australia was that disappointing employment growth and low inflation would yet prompt the Reserve Bank to ease policy again.
Figures on weekly earnings this Thursday may, or may not, add to the risk with forecasts of the likely annual growth rate ranging from a tolerable 4.0 percent to a fiesty 4.6 percent.
Median forecasts saw growth accelerating to 4.3 percent from 3.9 percent in Q4, still below the RBA's danger zone of 4.5-5.0 percent and thus, of itself, not an obstacle to a cut.
However, analysts also reckoned that data due on the real side of the economy would show activity picked up in Q1.

Building approvals on Thursday should confirm the ongoing recovery in the housing market with a 2.0 percent rise expected for March and talk it could be as high as 15 percent due to one-off developments such as the Olympic village.
Retail trade for March, on Friday, was seen flat after strong gains the previous two months.
Such an outcome for the month would still ensure real retail trade rose a healthy 2.4 percent in the quarter, which would add around 0.5-0.6 point to GDP growth in the March quarter.

There were few clues about near term policy from a speech by RBA deputy governor Stephen Grenville. But he did reiterate the bank's determination to keep inflation down through good monetary policy and a strict adherence to its 2-3 percent target for inflation. He identified a number of reasons why the bank was confident it could keep inflation low but also emphasised the economy could not exceed accepted speed limits without putting that goal at risk. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
